organizations.name: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: Ten independent experts (incl. one from each P5 state) hired by the UNSC to support the Taliban and al-Qaeda/IS sanctions regimes; two reports a year on AQ/IS and one on the Taliban; consults member-state intelligence services; report under discussion went to press 31 May 2024.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Hosts describe it as a terrorist organization running a state; retains a suicide-bomber capability in its armed forces, uses al-Qaeda instruction manuals, spends heavily on military/security; profits from opium stockpiles and meth.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Per UN report: training camps in 12 of 34 Afghan provinces, incl. new camps in Kandahar and Takhar; safe houses, madrasa, media operations centre, weapons storage; uses Afghanistan as a 'permissive haven'; leader Saif al-Adel in Tehran.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS)
organizations.notes: UN estimates ~200 members (hosts skeptical); 'hundreds' supported the Oct 2023 TTP cross-border attack; AQIS training changed TTP tactics.

organizations.name: Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan
aliases: movement of the Taliban in Pakistan
organizations.notes: Largest (foreign) terrorist group in Afghanistan per UN, ~6,000-6,500 fighters; given NATO-calibre weapons and night vision by the Taliban; trained in al-Qaeda camps in Kandahar, Nangarhar, Takhar.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Runs Paktia, Paktika, Khost; hosted al-Qaeda camps there since before 9/11; controls and profits from the methamphetamine trade; US-designated FTO; liaises with Iranian intelligence.

organizations.name: Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP)
organizations.notes: Only foreign group the Taliban actually oppose; recruited disaffected TTP in the past; Taliban fear TTP or ETIM making common cause with it.

organizations.name: Jamaat Ansarullah
aliases: movement of the Taliban in Tajikistan
organizations.notes: Tajik group given new military vehicles, weaponry and equipment by the Taliban and deployed on the Tajikistan border in Badakhshan; a Tajik commander controlled seven districts in Badakhshan.

organizations.name: Turkestan Islamic Party
organizations.notes: Uyghur group sheltered by the Taliban; relationship with TTP; Taliban worry about its links to ISKP; leader Abdul Haq al-Turkistani designated as member of al-Qaeda's Shura Majlis.

organizations.name: Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan
organizations.notes: Host expects it to re-initiate activities in Uzbekistan; historically clashed with the Pakistani Taliban, mediated by Sirajuddin Haqqani.

organizations.name: Tehreek-e-Jihad Pakistan
organizations.notes: Hosts assess it is a TTP cutout created for plausible deniability.

organizations.name: Katiba Umar Farooq
organizations.notes: Mentioned in UN report as present in Afghanistan; Fitton-Brown sees it as preparing for 'live action'.

organizations.name: General Directorate of Intelligence
organizations.notes: Taliban intelligence service; took Abu Ikhlas al-Masri into 'protective custody' late Nov 2023.

organizations.name: Iranian intelligence
organizations.notes: Hosts Saif al-Adel in Tehran; liaises with the Haqqani Network.

organizations.name: Government of Pakistan
organizations.notes: Sponsored the Afghan Taliban for 'strategic depth'; hosts say it is the frog to the Taliban's scorpion.

organizations.name: Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction
organizations.notes: Roggio compared its district-control data (three months lagged) to his own.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP)
organizations.notes: Cited as a possible origin for external al-Qaeda attacks.

events.description: UN Monitoring Team Taliban report went to press (published shortly before the episode); documents two additional provinces (Kandahar, Takhar) with al-Qaeda training camps, 12 of 34 provinces total.
actors: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team

events.description: Saif al-Adel called for al-Qaeda fighters to migrate to Afghanistan (after the report's 31 May press date).
Large TTP cross-border attack into Chitral, Pakistan, involving about 1,000 TTP fighters supported by 'hundreds' of AQIS.
Abu Ikhlas al-Masri taken into 'protective custody' by the Taliban General Directorate of Intelligence in late November 2023.
Abu Ikhlas al-Masri freed from Bagram prison when the Taliban took control of the site in summer 2021.
Noor Wali Mehsud renewed his pledge of allegiance to the Afghan Taliban emir days after the Taliban took control of Afghanistan.
CENTCOM commander Gen. McKenzie testified to Congress that US intelligence in Afghanistan was reduced to 1-2% of what it was with a presence there.
US raided al-Qaeda camps in Shorabak district, Kandahar, killing almost 200 al-Qaeda fighters; US estimate then revised from '50-100' to ~300.
Hibatullah Akhundzada's decree banning poppy cultivation; followed by an anti-narcotics act in 2023. UN says huge opium stockpiles still released along routes controlled by senior Taliban.
UNSC resolution 1988 separated the Taliban sanctions regime from the al-Qaeda regime; since then the UN has not called the Taliban a terrorist group.
US State Department designated TIP leader Abdul Haq al-Turkistani, naming him a member of al-Qaeda's Shura Majlis (host unsure whether 2007 or 2008).
Abu Muhammad al-Masri assassinated in Tehran (host says 'I believe 2012'; widely reported as Aug 2020). Photos of him and two other AQ leaders as tourists in Tehran date to 2006.
TTP seized Buner district within 50-60 miles of Islamabad before the Pakistani state took action against it (date inferred from context; host says 'almost 15 years ago').

key_claims: Al-Qaeda runs training camps in 12 of 34 Afghan provinces (new: Kandahar, Takhar) plus safe houses, a madrasa, a media centre and a weapons depot; infrastructure is growing, not shrinking, and the UN's ~200 AQIS figure is too low.
The Taliban's 'restraint' of al-Qaeda consists of al-Qaeda choosing not to embarrass its host with an external attack; al-Qaeda is exercising strategic patience, not being suppressed.

Saif al-Adel leads al-Qaeda from Tehran, liaises with Iranian intelligence, the Taliban and the Haqqani Network, and Iranian intelligence and the Haqqanis liaise with each other ('a joined-up operation between Iran and Afghanistan').
The Taliban do not regard the TTP as terrorists; they pay Noor Wali Mehsud a salary, give the TTP NATO-calibre weapons and night vision, and let AQIS train and fight alongside it (Chitral, Oct 2023).
The Taliban arm Jamaat Ansarullah on the Tajik border and shelter TIP/ETIM and the IMU, keeping them 'gainfully employed' as a protection racket against hostile neighbours.
The Haqqani Network runs Paktia/Paktika/Khost and the meth trade; al-Qaeda's historical camps there are absent from the UN report, which Roggio attributes to a reporting gap.
Both hosts conclude the Taliban itself is the dominant terrorist organization in Afghanistan, not ISKP, and that partnering with it against ISKP is 'like having the flu and taking a shot of malaria'.
